claim: Hippocampal CA2 pyramidal neurons show unusually strong excitation by their distal dendritic inputs from entorhinal cortex (EC).
source: In contrast to most other cortical and hippocampal neurons, hippocampal CA2 pyramidal neurons show unusually strong excitation by their distal dendritic inputs from entorhinal cortex (EC).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by experimental data comparing CA2 and CA1 responses to PP stimulation shown in Figure 1.

claim: The ability of EC inputs to drive CA2 AP output requires the firing of local dendritic Na+ spikes.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that the ability of these EC inputs to drive CA2 AP output requires the firing of local dendritic Na+ spikes.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data using TTX application to block dendritic spikes (Figures 5, 6).

claim: CA2 dendritic geometry contributes to the efficient coupling of dendritic Na+ spikes to AP output.
source: Furthermore, we find that CA2 dendritic geometry contributes to the efficient coupling of dendritic Na+ spikes to AP output.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by computational modeling based on morphological reconstructions shown in Figure 10.

claim: Dendritic spikes enable direct cortical inputs to overcome unfavorable distal synaptic locale to trigger axonal AP output.
source: These results provide a striking example of how dendritic spikes enable direct cortical inputs to overcome unfavorable distal synaptic locale to trigger axonal AP output and thereby enable efficient cortico-hippocampal information flow.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the abstract that integrates multiple experimental findings from the study.

claim: CA2 pyramidal neurons are crucial for social memory.
source: Nonetheless, these neurons have recently been shown to be crucial for social memory (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Stevenson and Caldwell, 2014) and aggression (Pagani et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CA2 pyramidal neurons are crucial for aggression.
source: Nonetheless, these neurons have recently been shown to be crucial for social memory (Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Stevenson and Caldwell, 2014) and aggression (Pagani et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: PP inputs from EC form weak excitatory synaptic connections at the distal dendrites of CA1 PNs located in stratum lacunosum-moleculare (SLM).
source: Thus, whereas the perforant path (PP) inputs from the EC form weak excitatory synaptic connections at the distal dendrites of CA1 PNs located in stratum lacunosum-moleculare (SLM), PP inputs to CA2 PNs provide a much stronger excitatory drive (Chevaleyre and Siegelbaum, 2010).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PP inputs to CA2 PNs provide a much stronger excitatory drive compared to CA1 PNs.
source: Thus, whereas the perforant path (PP) inputs from the EC form weak excitatory synaptic connections at the distal dendrites of CA1 PNs located in stratum lacunosum-moleculare (SLM), PP inputs to CA2 PNs provide a much stronger excitatory drive (Chevaleyre and Siegelbaum, 2010).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work and experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: The Schaffer collateral (SC) inputs to CA2 are relatively weak and dominated by powerful feed-forward inhibition.
source: In contrast the Schaffer collateral (SC) inputs to CA2 are relatively weak and dominated by powerful feed-forward inhibition (Chevaleyre and Siegelbaum, 2010).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Individual CA2 PNs provide stronger excitatory drive to CA1 compared to the weaker influence of single CA3 SC inputs.
source: Finally, individual CA2 PNs provide stronger excitatory drive to CA1 compared to the weaker influence of single CA3 SC inputs (Chevaleyre and Siegelbaum, 2010).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The CA2 region functions as the nexus of a powerful disynaptic circuit (EC → CA2 → CA1), directly linking EC input to hippocampal CA1 output.
source: Such properties enable the CA2 region to function as the nexus of a powerful disynaptic circuit (EC → CA2 → CA1), directly linking EC input to hippocampal CA1 output (Jones and McHugh, 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: PP inputs to distal dendrites in CA2 reliably initiate dendritic Na+ spikes that are necessary to trigger axonal AP output in response to a single or a burst of PP stimuli.
source: In this study, we report the PP inputs to distal dendrites in CA2 reliably initiate dendritic Na+ spikes that are necessary to trigger axonal AP output in response to a single or a burst of PP stimuli.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figures 2-6.

claim: Dendritic Na+ spikes in CA2 can overcome strong inhibition to elicit AP output.
source: Furthermore, these spikes can overcome strong inhibition to elicit AP output.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figure 9.

claim: Activation of PP inputs to distal dendrites of CA1 PNs with a single stimulus fail to elicit dendritic spikes or somatic APs.
source: In contrast, activation of PP inputs to distal dendrites of CA1 PNs with a single stimulus fail to elicit dendritic spikes or somatic APs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by experimental data in Figures 2-4.

claim: The distinct dendritic geometry of CA2 PNs contributes to the ability of CA2 neurons to efficiently couple dendritic Na+ spikes to AP output.
source: Through computational modeling based on morphological reconstructions of CA2 and CA1 PNs, we find that the distinct dendritic geometry of CA2 PNs contributes to the ability of CA2 neurons to efficiently couple dendritic Na+ spikes to AP output.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by computational modeling data in Figure 10.

claim: The sub-threshold EPSP amplitude in CA2 PNs evoked by PP stimulation was 5–6 times larger than that observed in CA1.
source: Consistent with our previous findings (Chevaleyre and Siegelbaum, 2010), the sub-threshold EPSP amplitude in CA2 PNs evoked by PP stimulation was 5–6 times larger than that observed in CA1 (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: In the vast majority of CA2 PNs tested (35/42 cells), a single electrical stimulus (up to 48 V) delivered to the PP was sufficient to elicit a large, fast AP that was >80 mV in amplitude when recorded in the CA2 soma.
source: In the vast majority of CA2 PNs tested (35/42 cells), a single electrical stimulus (up to 48 V) delivered to the PP was sufficient to elicit a large, fast AP that was >80 mV in amplitude when recorded in the CA2 soma (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: CA1 PNs never fired a spike in response to a single PP stimulus, even at strengths up to 60 V.
source: By contrast, CA1 PNs never fired a spike in response to a single PP stimulus, even at strengths up to 60 V (with the stimulating electrode located within 50 μm of the CA1 PN as in our CA2 recordings), but required a burst of high-frequency PP stimuli to fire APs (e.g. Figure 2D, Figure 3B, Figure 4B), consistent with a previous report (Jarsky et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D, 3B, 4B, and citation to previous work.

claim: The electrically evoked APs in CA2 were eliminated by blockade of fast glutamatergic synaptic transmission, using bath application of NBQX (20 μM) and D-APV (50 μM).
source: The electrically evoked APs were eliminated by blockade of fast glutamatergic synaptic transmission, using bath application of NBQX (20 μM) and D-APV (50 μM) (Figure 1D, n = 4).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The spikes in CA2 were driven by synaptic excitation, not by direct electrical stimulation of CA2 dendrites.
source: Thus, the spikes were driven by synaptic excitation, not by direct electrical stimulation of CA2 dendrites.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and is inferred from the pharmacological blockade experiment showing that glutamate receptor antagonists eliminate the spikes.

claim: The largest EPSP observed in the CA2 PN soma was ∼11 mV below the voltage threshold of AP output in response to somatic current injection.
source: The efficient triggering of action potential output from CA2 PNs in response to PP stimulation is surprising given that the largest EPSP observed in the CA2 PN soma was ∼11 mV below the voltage threshold of AP output in response to somatic current injection (Figure 1G–I, see also Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G-I and 2C.

claim: Nearly all CA2 PNs fired APs in response to a PP stimulus that was strong enough to induce a somatic EPSP greater than 15.6 ± 0.6 mV (ranging from 7.7–20.3 mV, n = 27).
source: Nearly all CA2 PNs fired APs in response to a PP stimulus that was strong enough to induce a somatic EPSP greater than 15.6 ± 0.6 mV (ranging from 7.7–20.3 mV, n = 27, Figure 1G–I).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1G-I.

claim: In a subset of CA2 PNs (n = 9/42 cells), PP stimuli that were just below threshold for eliciting an AP evoked a somatic voltage response with a rapidly rising phase of depolarization not seen in voltage responses evoked by weaker PP stimuli.
source: In a subset of CA2 PNs (n = 9/42 cells), PP stimuli that were just below threshold for eliciting an AP evoked a somatic voltage response with a rapidly rising phase of depolarization not seen in voltage responses evoked by weaker PP stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The rapidly rising depolarization in CA2 PNs is similar to the somatic spikelets associated with dendritic Na+ spikes reported in other studies.
source: This rapidly rising depolarization is similar to the somatic spikelets associated with dendritic Na+ spikes reported in other studies (Losonczy and Magee, 2006; Losonczy et al., 2008; Remy et al., 2009; Muller et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: As the EPSP in CA2 reached values around 15–20 mV, dV/dt increased sharply in a non-linear manner, suggesting that large EPSPs are sufficient to trigger a non-linear membrane response that likely reflects the firing of a dendritic spike.
source: Although dV/dt initially increased linearly with peak EPSP amplitude, as the EPSP reached values around 15–20 mV, dV/dt increased sharply in a non-linear manner. This suggests that large EPSPs are sufficient to trigger a non-linear membrane response that likely reflects the firing of a dendritic spike (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The 20–80% rise time of the EPSP decreased non-linearly as the peak EPSP amplitude reached values above ∼15 mV.
source: Consistent with this view, the 20–80% rise time of the EPSP also decreased non-linearly as the peak EPSP amplitude reached values above ∼15 mV (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: A phase-plane plot of dV/dt vs membrane voltage showed that APs induced by PP stimulation in CA2 PNs consistently exhibited an initial rapid dV/dt signal at potentials sub-threshold to the main spike.
source: In agreement with this idea, a phase-plane plot of dV/dt vs membrane voltage showed that APs induced by PP stimulation in CA2 PNs consistently exhibited an initial rapid dV/dt signal at potentials sub-threshold to the main spike (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: An early rapid phase of depolarization was not observed when APs in CA2 PNs were elicited by somatic current injection, suggesting that they represent dendritic spikes.
source: Such an early rapid phase of depolarization was not observed when APs were elicited by somatic current injection, suggesting that they do indeed represent dendritic spikes (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The AP threshold (defined as the somatic voltage at which dV/dt reached 50 V/s) was significantly lower in response to PP stimulation (−51.6 ± 1.0 mV) compared to somatic current injection (−44.3 ± 0.8 mV, n = 17, p < 0.001) in CA2 PNs.
source: Furthermore, we compared the threshold to fire APs induced by PP stimulation with that induced by somatic current injection. The AP threshold (defined as the somatic voltage at which dV/dt reached 50 V/s) was significantly lower in response to PP stimulation (−51.6 ± 1.0 mV) compared to somatic current injection (−44.3 ± 0.8 mV, n = 17, p < 0.001; Figure 2C), indicating that dendritic spikes may indeed be required for PP input to trigger somatic APs.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In CA1 PNs, neither somatic voltage recordings nor phase-plane plots showed evidence of a spikelet in response to PP-evoked action potentials.
source: In marked contrast with our results with CA2 PNs, neither our somatic voltage recordings nor phase-plane plots showed evidence of a spikelet (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Individual spikes, phase-plane plots, and voltage threshold of somatic APs induced by PP stimulation were identical with those induced by somatic current injections in CA1 PNs.
source: Moreover, individual spikes, phase-plane plots, and voltage threshold of somatic APs induced by PP stimulation were identical with those induced by somatic current injections (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: In CA1 PNs, somatic depolarization resulting from temporal summation of PP-evoked EPSPs, rather than dendritic spikes, drives AP output.
source: These results suggest that in CA1 PNs, somatic depolarization resulting from temporal summation of PP-evoked EPSPs, rather than dendritic spikes, drives AP output.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and is inferred from the experimental data showing no evidence of spikelets in CA1 PNs.

claim: Hyperpolarizing the somatic membrane to −82.5 ± 2.8 mV (n = 10) revealed that PP stimulation consistently evoked rapidly rising spikelets (dV/dt of 20.6 ± 2.6 V/s; n = 10) in CA2 PNs.
source: Strikingly, this revealed that PP stimulation consistently evoked a rapidly rising spikelets (dV/dt of 20.6 ± 2.6 V/s; n = 10) in response to PP stimulation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When repeated single PP stimuli of a constant strength near the threshold for eliciting somatic APs were applied, the CA2 PN membrane response often fluctuated between a full-blown AP response and a spikelet.
source: When we applied repeated single PP stimuli of a constant strength near the threshold for eliciting somatic APs, the CA2 PN membrane response often fluctuated between a full-blown AP response and a spikelet (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Overlaying responses in CA2 PNs showed that the spikelets preceded the full-blown APs, suggesting that the dendritic spikes triggered the full-blown APs.
source: Overlaying these responses showed that the spikelets preceded the full-blown APs (Figure 3A), suggesting that the dendritic spikes triggered the full-blown APs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Spikelets were not observed in CA1 soma upon membrane hyperpolarization.
source: In marked contrast, we failed to observe spikelets in CA1 soma upon membrane hyperpolarization (Figure 3B, n = 9).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Local application of TTX (1 µM) to the soma of CA2 PNs revealed the consistent presence of spikelets (dV/dt = 36.4 ± 3.0 V/s, n = 8) in response to PP stimuli.
source: In CA2 PNs, this manipulation revealed the consistent presence of spikelets (dV/dt = 36.4 ± 3.0 V/s, n = 8) in response to PP stimuli (Figure 4C–I).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C-I.

claim: Spikelets in CA2 PNs provide a substantial somatic depolarization (33.6 ± 2.8 mV, n = 8) that would normally trigger a somatic action potential in the absence of TTX.
source: These spikelets provide a substantial somatic depolarization (33.6 ± 2.8 mV, n = 8) that would normally trigger a somatic action potential in the absence of TTX.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is based on experimental data.

claim: Spikelets were not observed with TTX applied to the soma of CA1 PNs.
source: In contrast, we failed to observe spikelets with TTX applied to the soma of CA1 PNs (Figure 4A,B, n = 4).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Single PP stimuli are sufficient to evoke prominent dendritic spikes, which result in high-amplitude somatic spikelets in CA2 but not CA1 PNs.
source: Taken together, we conclude that single PP stimuli are sufficient to evoke prominent dendritic spikes, which result in high-amplitude somatic spikelets in CA2 but not CA1 PNs.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the text that integrates multiple experimental findings.

claim: The threshold to fire a somatic AP with PP stimulation is negative to the threshold with somatic current injection in CA2 PNs, indicating the necessity of dendritic spikes.
source: As discussed above, one indication for the necessity of dendritic spikes is our finding that the threshold to fire a somatic AP with PP stimulation is negative to the threshold with somatic current injection (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Local application of TTX to the proximal dendrites of CA2 PNs fully blocked the ability of single PP stimuli to elicit somatic APs.
source: Indeed, this manipulation fully blocked the ability of single PP stimuli to elicit somatic APs (Figure 5A–D, n = 6).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-D.

claim: After blockade of dendritic Na+ spikes, the EPSP evoked by strong PP stimulation maximally depolarized the soma by ∼20 mV positive to the resting potential (−70 to −73 mV), below the threshold for driving AP output by somatic current injection.
source: After blockade of dendritic Na+ spikes, the EPSP evoked by strong PP stimulation maximally depolarized the soma by ∼20 mV positive to the resting potential (−70 to −73 mV) (Figure 5D), below the threshold for driving AP output by somatic current injection.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Local TTX application to dendrites exerted a selective effect on dendritic excitability and did not alter PP synaptic transmission or somatic excitability.
source: Importantly, the local TTX application exerted a selective effect on dendritic excitability and did not alter PP synaptic transmission or somatic excitability. Thus, there was no change in the sub-threshold PP EPSP or AP firing in response to somatic current injection (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-H.

claim: Dendritic spikes in CA2 PNs are mediated by TTX-sensitive voltage-gated Na+ channels.
source: These results strongly suggest that dendritic spikes in CA2 PNs are mediated by TTX-sensitive voltage-gated Na+ channels (see below for additional evidence) and are necessary for somatic AP initiation with a single PP stimulus.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and is inferred from the TTX blockade experiments.

claim: Dendritic spikes in CA2 PNs are necessary for somatic AP initiation with a single PP stimulus.
source: These results strongly suggest that dendritic spikes in CA2 PNs are mediated by TTX-sensitive voltage-gated Na+ channels (see below for additional evidence) and are necessary for somatic AP initiation with a single PP stimulus.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data showing that TTX blockade of dendritic spikes prevents AP firing.

claim: A phase-plane plot revealed the presence of an early rapid rising voltage response preceding the full-blown somatic spikes in response to a 50 Hz burst of 5 PP stimuli in CA2 PNs.
source: However, a phase-plane plot revealed the presence of an early rapid rising voltage response preceding the full-blown somatic spikes in response to a 50 Hz burst of 5 PP stimuli (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Application of somatic TTX revealed the consistent presence of somatic spikelets in CA2 PNs in response to PP burst stimuli.
source: Moreover, application of somatic TTX revealed the consistent presence of somatic spikelets (Figure 6C,D, n = 6) that precede AP initiation in the absence of TTX (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Local application of TTX to the proximal dendrites fully blocked the ability of PP burst stimuli to drive AP output in CA2 PNs.
source: Importantly, local application of TTX to the proximal dendrites fully blocked the ability of PP burst stimuli to drive AP output (Figure 6E,F, n = 3).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E,F.

claim: Under the conditions of the experiments, cortically-driven dendritic Na+ spikes were necessary for AP output in CA2 PNs with either single or bursts of PP input.
source: Thus, under the conditions of our experiments, cortically-driven dendritic Na+ spikes were necessary for AP output in CA2 PNs with either single or bursts of PP input.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the text that integrates multiple experimental findings.

claim: In CA1, a measurable PS was never observed following the first PP stimulus and was only detected during the later stimuli in a burst, resulting in a latency to firing of 20 ms or more.
source: In CA1, a measurable PS was never observed following the first PP stimulus and was only detected during the later stimuli in a burst, resulting in a latency to firing of 20 ms or more (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The PS amplitude in CA2 was largest in response to the first stimulus of a burst and gradually diminished with successive stimuli.
source: In contrast, the PS amplitude in CA2 was largest in response to the first stimulus of a burst and gradually diminished with successive stimuli (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decrease in PS response in CA2 was not due to synaptic depression because the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) of PP synapses in CA2 PNs exhibited facilitation rather than depression (PPR = 1.39 ± 0.06, n = 17).
source: The decrease in PS response was not due to synaptic depression because the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) of PP synapses in CA2 PNs exhibited facilitation rather than depression (PPR = 1.39 ± 0.06, n = 17).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data.

claim: CA2 PNs fired precisely and immediately in response to PP stimulation (latency of the first PS = 4.4 ± 0.1 ms, n = 5), suggesting that dendritic Na+ spikes enable CA2 PNs to respond rapidly to EC burst firing with a high degree of temporal fidelity.
source: Thus, CA2 PNs fired precisely and immediately in response to PP stimulation (latency of the first PS = 4.4 ± 0.1 ms, n = 5), suggesting that dendritic Na+ spikes enable CA2 PNs to respond rapidly to EC burst firing with a high degree of temporal fidelity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data.

claim: CA2 dendrites generated an active excitatory current response to PP stimulation, manifested as a negative field voltage response in recordings from SR.
source: CA2 dendrites generated an active excitatory current response to PP stimulation, manifested as a negative field voltage response in recordings from SR (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: PP stimuli never evoked an active response in SR of CA1 or CA3.
source: In contrast, PP stimuli never evoked an active response in SR of CA1 or CA3.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is based on experimental observations.

claim: The amplitude of the active response in SR was correlated with PS size in SP (somatic spike; R = 0.91) in CA2.
source: Importantly, the amplitude of the active response in SR was correlated with PS size in SP (somatic spike; R = 0.91, Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The SR potential preceded the PS in SP in CA2.
source: Furthermore, the SR potential preceded the PS in SP (Figure 7D), suggesting that dendritic Na+ spikes precede somatic APs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The difference in latency between SR and SP active responses was correlated with the distance between the dendritic and somatic recording sites in CA2.
source: Moreover, the difference in latency between SR and SP active responses was correlated with the distance between the dendritic and somatic recording sites (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The dendrites of CA2 PNs, but not CA1 or CA3 PNs, fire spikes that propagate to the soma of CA2 PNs to trigger AP output.
source: These results suggest that the dendrites of CA2 PNs, but not CA1 or CA3 PNs, fire spikes that propagate to the soma of CA2 PNs to trigger AP output.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the text that integrates multiple experimental findings.

claim: CA2 dendrites had distinct electrophysiological properties from CA1 dendrites, including lack of voltage sag, a late depolarizing response to hyperpolarizing current injection characteristic of Ih, and lack of AP adaptation.
source: CA2 dendrites had distinct electrophysiological properties from CA1 dendrites, including lack of voltage sag, a late depolarizing response to hyperpolarizing current injection characteristic of Ih, and lack of AP adaptation (CA2 recordings of Figure 8B compared to CA1 recordings in Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dendritic spikes could be reliably triggered by brief depolarizing current pulses in all CA2 dendrites examined, with a current threshold of 1.7 ± 0.2 nA (n = 10).
source: We found that dendritic spikes could be reliably triggered by brief depolarizing current pulses in all CA2 dendrites examined, with a current threshold of 1.7 ± 0.2 nA (n = 10) (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The dendritic spikes in CA2 were generated by voltage-gated Na+ channels as they were blocked by bath application of TTX (0.5 µM, n = 3).
source: Furthermore, the dendritic spikes were generated by voltage-gated Na+ channels as they were blocked by bath application of TTX (0.5 µM, n = 3; Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: A single PP synaptic stimulus was able to evoke a dendritic spike in CA2 dendrites.
source: Finally, the dendritic recordings directly demonstrated that a single PP synaptic stimulus was able to evoke a dendritic spike (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D,E.

claim: Bath applied D-APV (50 μM) did not block dendritic spikes elicited by a single PP stimulus in CA2 PNs.
source: However, we found that bath applied D-APV (50 μM) did not block dendritic spikes elicited by a single PP stimulus (Figure 8—figure supplement 2) and failed to inhibit the PS in the CA2 PN layer elicited with strong current stimulating pulses (>24 V; Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: D-APV produced a small decrease (20%) in EPSP amplitude in CA2 PNs.
source: However, D-APV did produce a small decrease (20%) in EPSP amplitude (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2.

claim: NMDAR activation is not required for dendritic spike initiation or AP output in response to PP activation in CA2 PNs.
source: Thus NMDAR activation is not required for dendritic spike initiation or AP output in response to PP activation in CA2 PNs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and is inferred from the D-APV experiments.

claim: For stimulus strengths above 12 V, the PP PSP in CA2 was significantly enhanced by GABAR antagonists, indicating that PP stimulation elicited strong inhibition.
source: For stimulus strengths above 12 V, the PP PSP was significantly enhanced by the GABAR antagonists, indicating that PP stimulation did indeed elicit strong inhibition (Figure 9A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: At an intermediate stimulus strength of 24 V, the PP-evoked PSP depolarized the membrane by only 6.6 ± 0.9 mV with inhibition intact, whereas the PSP size increased to 11.7 ± 1.3 mV when inhibition was blocked (p < 0.001, n = 10).
source: At an intermediate stimulus strength of 24 V, the PP-evoked PSP depolarized the membrane by only 6.6 ± 0.9 mV with inhibition intact, whereas the PSP size increased to 11.7 ± 1.3 mV when inhibition was blocked (p < 0.001, n = 10).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is based on experimental data.

source: Even at maximum strength (52 V), the PSP amplitude only reached 8.4 ± 1.1 mV with inhibition intact (ranging from 4.3 mV to 13.6 mV, n = 9, excluding responses with dendritic Na+ spikes or APs).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and is based on experimental data.

claim: A single PP stimulus was able to evoke a PS in the CA2 cell body layer even with inhibition present.
source: Surprisingly, however, extracellular field recordings showed that a single PP stimulus was, in fact, able to evoke a PS in the CA2 cell body layer even with inhibition present (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The stimulation threshold for eliciting a PS was higher and the PS amplitude was reduced when inhibition was intact compared to when inhibition was blocked in CA2.
source: As expected, the stimulation threshold for eliciting a PS was higher and the PS amplitude was reduced when inhibition was intact compared to when inhibition was blocked (Figure 9B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B.

claim: A single PP stimulus was able to elicit AP firing in CA2 when inhibition was present, although with a reduced probability compared to when inhibition was blocked.
source: Somatic whole-cell recordings confirmed that a single PP stimulus was able to elicit AP firing when inhibition was present, although with a reduced probability compared to when inhibition was blocked (Figure 9C,D).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C,D.

claim: With inhibition intact, CA2 PNs fired APs following somatic PSPs whose peak amplitude, on average, reached a threshold of 10.99 ± 0.59 mV (ranging from 8.6–13.6 mV, n = 6).
source: With inhibition intact, CA2 PNs fired APs following somatic PSPs whose peak amplitude, on average, reached a threshold of 10.99 ± 0.59 mV (Figure 9E,F, ranging from 8.6–13.6 mV, n = 6).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the text and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9E,F.

claim: In the presence of inhibition, repeated trials of PP stimulation using a constant stimulus strength near threshold elicited variable responses, with full-blown APs, spikelets (dendritic Na+ spikes), or sub-threshold PSPs in CA2 PNs.
